title: Start from a one-sentence premise: you are X, you must Y, before Z
text: Before writing any label, chapter or board line, write the premise as one sentence with a role, an action and a stake: "You are the last lantern carrier and must relight 6 shrines before the ghosts wake." Every other line in the game should trace back to it. If the premise needs two sentences, the story is too big for a 1-8 minute play.
use_when: the concept is chosen and you are about to write the story, labels or chapters
do: Write role + action + stake in one sentence
Use the premise as sentence 1 or 2 of the intro card
Check each label against it: does this line serve the premise?
avoid: Premises that are only a setting ("A spooky temple")
Two goals at once ("save the village and win the race and find the treasure")
source: Schell, The Art of Game Design

title: Split checkpoints into three acts: arrive, trouble, triumph
text: Map the checkpoint count onto a short three-act shape. With 4 checkpoints use 1-2-1, with 6 use 2-2-2, with 8 use 2-4-2, with 10 use 3-4-3. Act 1 labels set up the world and the task ("Enter the reef"), act 2 labels raise trouble ("Swim past the eels"), act 3 labels pay off ("Wake the pearl queen"). The portal is the curtain call, not a fourth act.
use_when: writing 4-10 checkpoint labels for a runner with narrative as a feeling
do: Decide the act split before writing labels
Put the hardest hazard in act 2 and the payoff label in act 3
Make the act 3 labels name the thing promised on the intro card
avoid: Ten labels at one emotional level
Using act 1 to explain backstory instead of moving

title: Quest chain: each checkpoint makes the next one possible
text: A quest chain links stops by cause: "Wake the bell keeper", "Ring the old bell", "Open the river gate", "Free the boats". Nothing is carried or unlocked by the engine; the checkpoint order already forces the sequence, so the words only need to imply that each step leads to the next. This makes 5-7 checkpoints feel like one task instead of a list.
use_when: the brief wants a story with purpose and the route has 5-7 checkpoints
do: Let each label imply the result of the previous one
Show the change in scenery (a gate model beside "Open the river gate")
avoid: Saying a door really unlocks or an item is needed (no inventory)
Chains longer than 7 links in a short play

title: Rescue structure: find each captive, then go home through the portal
text: Rescue is the easiest story to read: each checkpoint is someone or something freed ("Free the first kitten"), hazards are what holds them (thorns, a curse ring, fire), and the portal is home. Put a still model of each captive beside its checkpoint so the label points at something visible. For kids use animals or toys; for adults use villagers or spirits.
use_when: a runner for kids or families, or any brief that says "help" or "save"
do: Count the captives in the goal line ("Free 5 kittens, then go home")
Show each captive as a scenery model at its checkpoint
avoid: Captives that follow you (the engine has no followers)
Rescue from violence in kids games; use cages, sleep spells, ice

title: Escape structure: the place is closing, the portal is the only way out
text: In an escape the danger is behind you and the portal is the exit. Labels count down places passed ("Out of the cell", "Past the kitchen", "Up the stairs", "The last door") and hazards are the closing threat (lava, alarm rings). A time limit fits naturally ("before the volcano blows"), so set timeLimit and mention it once in the story. Escape suits challenge, sensation and races.
use_when: a runner that should feel urgent, or a race
do: Write labels as places passed, not tasks done
Name the time limit in story words ("before sunrise")
avoid: Calm wandering words in an escape
A threat that is described but never shown; place hazards or scenery for it

title: Delivery structure: you carry something precious from start to finish
text: A delivery story gives one object the whole journey: a lantern flame, a letter, a dragon egg. The object exists only in words (the engine has no carrying), so state it on the intro card ("You carry the last warm ember") and let labels be the stops on the way ("Shelter from the snow", "Cross the frozen lake", "Reach the cold village"). The portal is the handover.
use_when: a runner with a journey feeling, a tour, or a gentle family story
do: Name the carried thing on the intro card
Make the last label or the goal the handover ("Bring the ember to the village")
avoid: Rules or labels that say "do not drop it" (nothing can be dropped)
Asking players to hold a real object while walking in MR

title: Collection structure: a numbered set the player completes
text: Collection works when the set has a clear count and a reason: "5 lost stars to put back in the sky". Touching a checkpoint is the collecting, so labels can repeat a pattern on purpose ("Star 1: the well", "Star 2: the windmill"). Give the set a payoff in the last label or goal ("Light up the sky"). Kids love counting up, and the HUD already shows checkpoint progress.
use_when: a runner for kids, families or first-time VR players, or a submission feeling
do: Use the same noun with a number plus a place
Say the total on the intro card and in the goal
avoid: Collecting with no reason or payoff
Promising to use the collected things later (no inventory)

title: Tour structure: each checkpoint is one sight with one fact or feeling
text: A tour treats checkpoints as stops on a guided walk: "See the floating market", "Visit the spirit house", "Watch the elephants bathe". Each label names the sight and the vignette beside it shows it. Add no threat words; use hazards lightly as natural obstacles (puddles, sleeping dogs). Tours suit tourists, seniors, educators and brands showing a place.
use_when: tourists, school visits, brand showcases or a submission or discovery brief
do: One sight per label, named plainly
Let the intro card say where the tour goes and how many stops
avoid: Packing several facts into one label
Danger words in a relaxing tour

title: Mystery with a reveal at the end: a clue in each label, the answer in the last
text: A short mystery plants a question on the intro card ("Who stole the moon?") and lets each label add a clue the scenery shows ("Follow the silver footprints", "Check the empty nest"). The last checkpoint label gives the answer ("The owl kept it for her chicks"). The reveal must sit in the last label (or the boss intro in battle), because the engine has no ending screen to write on.
use_when: a runner or battle with narrative or discovery, played solo or together (not a race)
do: Ask the question on the intro card
Make the last label the answer, not one more clue
avoid: Clues that need paragraphs
Reveals that need every label read, in a race where players skim

title: Battle arc across chapters: outskirts, defences, heart, boss
text: Across 3-6 chapters let the place move inward: chapter 1 at the edge ("The Frozen Pass"), middle chapters at the defences ("The Shield Wall", "The Hunting Grounds"), the last chapter at the boss's door ("Below the Throne"), then the boss. Moving through named places makes the fight feel like a journey even though the arena itself does not change.
use_when: writing chapter titles for a battle game
do: Read the titles in order: they should move closer to the boss
Use the theme (ice, lava, forest, neon, desert, dark) in the place names
avoid: Titles that are only numbers or difficulty words ("Hard Wave")
Jumping to the boss lair in chapter 1

title: Give each enemy kind a story meaning and name it in its chapter line
text: The engine has three foes, so the words decide who they are. Grunts are fast and weak: a swarm (imps, ice sprites, sand rats). Shields block from the front: a wall of guards (stone soldiers, palace guards). Beasts are big chargers: the boss's pet (a lava hound, a forest boar). Rain is a sky threat: hail, falling embers, a curse. Mention the main foe in its chapter line ("Stone guards lock shields at the gate") so players know what is coming. Re-check after choosing foes: falling danger only when rain is true, a big creature only when a beast is in that chapter.
use_when: writing chapter lines once each chapter's foes are chosen
do: Match the line to the main foe kind in that chapter
Name rain as weather or a curse when rain is true
avoid: Describing archers or flying foes (not in the engine)
Calling a chapter of grunts "the giants"

title: Tactics arc across boards: the piece changes because the story does
text: Boards should vary the piece, and each change needs a story reason: start as a knight sneaking in ("Leap the garden walls"), become a rook in the long halls ("Charge the straight corridors"), a bishop in the chapel ("Slip along the diagonal pews"), and end as the queen ("Take back the throne"). The piece change reads as growth or disguise, not as a rule change.
use_when: writing 3-6 board stories for a tactics game
do: Tie each piece to the place of that board
Save the queen or the king target for the last board
avoid: Board stories that ignore which piece the player is
Changing piece with no word about why

title: The boss is the story payoff: name it twice before it appears
text: A boss lands when players already know it. Name it on the intro card ("the Ash King sleeps under the mountain"), hint at it in a middle chapter line ("His hounds smell you"), then let boss.intro deliver ("The Ash King rises. End this."). A boss who appears without warning feels like a random big enemy, not an ending.
use_when: writing the story card, chapter lines and boss for a battle game
do: Mention the boss name on the intro card
Hint at it in one chapter line before the last
Write the boss intro as the climax sentence
avoid: A boss name first seen in boss.intro
A boss unrelated to the chapters' theme

title: Label length: English 2-5 words, Thai about 6-16 characters
text: English labels read best at 2-5 words and under about 24 characters ("Ring the old bell"). Thai has no spaces between words, so count characters: aim for about 6-16 Thai characters ("ตีระฆังเก่า", "จุดเทียนดวงแรก"). Thai labels over about 20 characters blur in a headset while walking. If a label needs a comma, it is two labels.
use_when: writing checkpoint labels in either language, especially for MR
do: Read the label aloud in under 2 seconds
Cut adjectives first, keep the verb and the noun
avoid: Thai full sentences with particles and pronouns as labels
Commas, brackets or two clauses in one label

title: Thai labels start with the verb too, and drop the pronoun
text: Thai naturally puts the verb first in commands, so labels should read like a friend telling you what to do: "ปลุกยักษ์วัด", "ข้ามสะพานหมอก", "ช่วยลูกเป็ด". Drop "คุณ", "เรา" and "จง"; they make the label long and stiff. Good: "จุดตะเกียง". Bad: "คุณจะต้องจุดตะเกียงให้สว่าง".
use_when: writing checkpoint labels with lang = th
do: Verb + object, sometimes + one place word
Everyday verbs: ไป, หา, ช่วย, ปลุก, จุด, ข้าม
avoid: "จง..." commands (sounds like a textbook)
Starting every label with "ด่านที่ 3:"

title: Numbered progress in labels when the set repeats: "Bell 2", "Last bell"
text: When checkpoints are a set (bells, stars, lanterns), a number in the label tells players how far they are: "Bell 1: the gate", "Bell 2: the pond", "Last bell: the tower". In Thai: "ระฆังที่ 1 ประตูวัด", "ระฆังสุดท้าย บนหอ". Use Arabic digits so every player reads them fast, and name the final one "Last" or "สุดท้าย" to signal the climax.
use_when: a collection or chain runner with repeated checkpoint types
do: Number + place for each repeat
Switch to "Last" for the final one
avoid: Numbers with no place (players cannot tell the stops apart)
Thai numerals in labels

title: Checkpoint labels: bad drafts and good rewrites
text: Bad "Checkpoint 2" becomes "Cross the rope bridge". Bad "Now you must find the very old ancient lantern" becomes "Find the old lantern". Bad "Talk to the monk" becomes "Visit the monk" (no dialogue). Bad "Pick up the key" becomes "Reach the key stone" (no carrying). Bad Thai "ท่านจงเสด็จไปยังศาลา" becomes "ไปที่ศาลา". Bad "Zone C" becomes "Into the bamboo".
use_when: reviewing a draft list of checkpoint labels
do: Rewrite any label that names a number, a zone or an impossible action
Keep the verb and the visible noun
avoid: Labels that only describe geography with no action
Labels copied from another game

title: Safe label verbs: actions done just by arriving
text: A checkpoint is touched by walking into it, so the best verbs happen on arrival: reach, enter, cross, visit, light, wake, ring, free, find, greet, bless, see, pass. In Thai: ไปถึง, เข้า, ข้าม, ไปหา, จุด, ปลุก, ตี (ระฆัง), ปล่อย, หา, ไหว้, ดู. Avoid verbs that need hands, buttons or speech: pick up, throw, open with a key, talk, ask, buy, build, shoot.
use_when: choosing verbs for checkpoint labels
do: Pick an arrival verb that fits the scenery at that stop
Vary verbs across the route
avoid: Hand verbs (pick up, throw, craft)
Speech verbs (ask, tell, answer)

title: Six labels starting with "Find" read like a shopping list
text: When every label opens with the same verb ("Find the cat", "Find the hat", "Find the bat"), players stop reading after the second. Unless it is a deliberate numbered set, vary the verb so each stop has its own moment: "Spot the cat", "Wake the owl", "Cross the creek", "Free the fox". In Thai, rotate between หา, ปลุก, ข้าม, ช่วย, จุด.
use_when: a draft label list where most labels share a first word
do: Use at least 3 different verbs in 5-7 labels
Keep repetition only for numbered sets
avoid: The same verb on every label by accident
Fancy synonyms that are harder to read ("Procure")

title: There is no ending screen: land the ending on the last label
text: The game card has no finish-message field, and the portal only ends the run with the score. So the story's ending must live in the last checkpoint label ("Return the moon to the sky") and in what the goal line promised. Make the last label the resolution, not another errand, and give the portal a meaning on the intro card ("then the gate takes you home").
use_when: writing the final checkpoint label and the intro card of a runner
do: Write the last label as the payoff
Name the portal's meaning on the intro card (home, the exit, the next world)
avoid: Planning a victory speech or ending text the engine cannot show
A last label that is a minor errand

title: Intro card in 4 short sentences: world, you, trouble, go
text: The story field is 2-4 sentences read once before play. A reliable shape: 1) the world ("The river spirits lost their lights."), 2) who you are ("You are the lantern child."), 3) the trouble and the stake ("The ghosts wake at midnight."), 4) the call to action ("Light 5 lanterns and get home."). With only 2 sentences, merge 1+2 and 3+4. Keep each sentence under about 15 words.
use_when: writing game.story in the build step or in a pc_battle or pc_tactics game card
do: Second person "you" from sentence 2
End on an action the player does right away
avoid: Opening with history and dates
A fifth sentence of lore

title: Goal, story and labels must agree on the numbers and the final thing
text: If the goal says "Light 5 lanterns" there must be 5 lantern labels, and the story must not say "6 shrines". If the boss is "the Frost Warden" on the card, boss.name must match exactly. Players trust the card; a mismatch reads as a bug. Check counts and names across goal, story, labels, chapter lines, board stories (against the targets and guards of each board) and boss before submitting.
use_when: the last check before submitting a build, pc_battle or pc_tactics answer
do: Count labels against the goal number
Use the exact same spelling for names everywhere
avoid: Vague counts in the story ("a few lanterns") while the goal says 5
A boss with two different names

title: Rules list: 3-4 items, one plain verb each, in play order
text: The schema allows up to 8 rules for a runner and 6 for PC battle and tactics, but players read 3-4. Order them as played: what to do, what to avoid, how to finish. Runner example: "Walk to the glowing points in order", "Red circles send you back", "Step into the gate to finish". Use plain mechanic words, with at most a story word in brackets.
use_when: writing game.rules in the build step
do: One rule per line, starting with a verb or the thing to avoid
Put the finish rule last
avoid: Rules that repeat the story
More than 5 rules for kids or first-time VR players

title: Write rules in plain words with the story word beside them
text: Rules must be understood by everyone, so lead with the mechanic and add the fiction once: "Do not step in red circles (the lava pools)", "Capture targets in order (the stolen jewels)", "Step out of the red rings (the dragon's fire)". Thai: "อย่าเหยียบวงแดง (บ่อลาวา)". The story word carries the theme; the plain words keep the rule clear.
use_when: rules for a themed game where the fiction renames hazards or targets
do: Mechanic first, story word in brackets
Reuse the story word from the labels
avoid: Only the story word ("Avoid the Ember Wounds")
Rules that hide what actually happens

title: In MR, one rule is always about walking safely
text: Walking players in a real room need one safety rule on the card: "Walk, do not run", or for battle "Step, do not jump". Thai: "เดินนะ ห้ามวิ่ง". Put it second or third, not first, so it is read without opening the card like a warning sign. It matters most in races, which make people speed up.
use_when: any MR game card, especially races and battle
do: Include a walk-not-run rule in MR
Word it kindly and short
avoid: Leaving safety only to staff
Long legal-style warnings on the card
source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

title: Rule lists that work for each genre
text: Runner: "Walk to the points in order", "Red circles send you back", "Finish at the gate". Battle on PC: "Click to swing, 3 hits make a combo", "Dash out of red rings", "Clear every chapter, then beat the boss". Battle in MR: "Swing your right controller like a sword", "Step out of red rings", "Beat the boss". Tactics: "Move like your chess piece", "Capture targets in order", "Never stop on a square a guard attacks".
use_when: writing rules for battle, tactics or runner
do: Name the input in plain words on PC
Start from 3 lines and add only what the brief needs
avoid: Explaining how every chess piece moves in the list
Rules about mechanics the genre lacks

title: Chapter title 1-3 words; chapter line one sentence under 12 words
text: Titles are names of places or moments ("The Ash Road", "Ember Storm", "ถ้ำลาวา"); lines are one present-tense sentence about what happens now ("The road splits and the hounds come running."). Thai lines stay under about 30 characters: "ฝนไฟตกลงมา หลบให้ทัน". The line shows as a chapter starts, mid-action, so it must read in 2 seconds.
use_when: writing the title and line of each battle chapter
do: Present tense, one sentence
Put the danger word near the start of the line
avoid: Lines that explain controls (use the rules list)
Titles over 3 words

title: Boss names: a title plus one strong noun, easy to shout
text: Good boss names are 2-4 words that say what the boss rules or is made of: "The Ash King", "Frost Warden", "Mother of Thorns", "ราชาเถ้าถ่าน", "เจ้าแม่น้ำแข็ง". Players and spectators should be able to shout it. Avoid apostrophes, invented syllables and names that only work in one language if the game may be made in the other.
use_when: writing boss.name for a battle game
do: Title + element or domain
Match the theme (lava, ice, forest, neon, desert, dark)
avoid: Random syllable names ("Xyrrthak")
Names of real gods, kings or religious figures

title: Boss intro: what wakes, then what you must do, in 1-2 short sentences
text: boss.intro is the climax line. Write it as an event and a call: "The Ash King rises from the ember throne. Break his crown." Thai: "ราชาเถ้าถ่านตื่นแล้ว ล้มมันให้ได้". Use 5-15 words. The boss fight is fixed (ring slams, summoned grunts, faster below half health), so promise a fight, not a special attack.
use_when: writing boss.intro for a battle game
do: Short event + imperative
Reuse the boss name exactly
avoid: Describing fire breath, flying or phases the engine does not have
Long villain speeches (no dialogue)

title: Board story: one line under 12 words naming the targets and the guards
text: A tactics board line says what the targets and guards are in story terms: "Steal the 3 crowns before the night watch turns." Thai: "ขโมยมงกุฎ 3 ชิ้น ก่อนยามหันมา". Mention a target count only if it matches the board's targets number. Use the piece's nature when it helps ("Leap the hedges, rider").
use_when: writing the story line of each tactics board
do: Target meaning + guard meaning in one line
Match any number to the board's targets
avoid: Lines about moves the piece cannot make
Lines that describe the room only

title: Give each chess piece a role that matches how it moves
text: The piece the player is should feel like a character: knight = a rider or a frog that jumps over things, bishop = a monk or a shadow sliding on diagonals, rook = a battering cart or a castle golem charging in straight lines, queen = the hero, free in every direction. Write the role into the board story ("As the monk, slip along the diagonal halls").
use_when: tactics boards where the brief wants fantasy or kids need a hook
do: Mention the role once per board
Pick roles that fit the theme (Thai temple: elephant, naga, temple cat)
avoid: Roles whose movement contradicts the piece (a "flying" rook)
Calling the player only "the knight piece" with no fiction

title: Save the king for the last board and call it the climax
text: Setting king: true on the final board makes the last target a king, a natural climax: "Corner the Rat King in his hall." Earlier boards build toward it ("His guards are getting nervous"). Thai: "ต้อนราชาหนูให้จนมุม". The intro card can name the king from the start so the last board pays it off.
use_when: the final board of a 3-6 board tactics game
do: king: true only on the last board
Name the king on the intro card
avoid: A king on board 1
A king never mentioned before the final board

title: A time limit needs a story reason: before sunrise, before the tide
text: If timeLimit is set, say why in the story ("Get out before the volcano wakes", "ก่อนพระอาทิตย์ขึ้น") and state the minutes once in the goal or rules ("You have 3 minutes"). A clock with a reason feels like tension; a clock without one feels like a test. For submission or young kids, prefer no time limit and no clock words.
use_when: a design with a time limit, or deciding whether to add one
do: Tie the timer to a world event
State the minutes once as a plain number
avoid: Hurry words in a relaxing game
Different times in the story and in timeLimit

title: Thai: write like a friendly person speaking, not a textbook
text: Use everyday polite spoken Thai: "ไปช่วยลูกช้างกัน", "ระวังวงแดงนะ". Avoid formal written words that feel like an exam or a government notice: "ปฏิบัติภารกิจ", "ดำเนินการ", "กรุณาหลีกเลี่ยง". Avoid royal register (ราชาศัพท์) entirely unless the creator asks for a royal story, and even then keep it respectful and short.
use_when: any text with lang = th
do: Read the line aloud: would a teacher or an older sibling say it?
Use ไป, มา, ช่วย, หา, ระวัง, เลย
avoid: ราชาศัพท์ and court language
Bureaucratic words (ดำเนินการ, ปฏิบัติ, ทำการ)

title: Thai pronouns: drop them, or use "เรา" for warmth
text: Thai sentences work without a subject, so most lines need no pronoun: "จุดตะเกียงให้ครบ 5 ดวง". When the intro card needs one, "คุณ" is neutral for adults and "เรา" makes kids and families feel included ("เราต้องช่วยลูกเต่ากลับบ้าน"). Avoid "ท่าน" (stiff) and "เจ้า" (old period drama, unless the theme is fantasy), and never use rude pronouns.
use_when: writing intro cards and lines in Thai
do: No pronoun in labels
คุณ for adults, เรา for kids and families
avoid: ท่าน in game text
Mixing คุณ and เรา on one card

title: Thai for kids 6-10: short common words, no heavy Pali or Sanskrit vocabulary
text: Children read slowly in a headset. Use words they know: "ผี" not "วิญญาณ", "ยักษ์" not "อสุรกาย", "ช่วย" not "กอบกู้", "บ้าน" not "ที่พำนัก". Keep lines to about 10-20 characters and add playful sound words sparingly ("ว้าว", "ปุ๊ง!"). Friendly creature names beat scary ones: "ผีน้อยขี้เหงา" works, while a folklore ghost famous for gore may frighten young kids.
use_when: lang = th and players are kids or families with young children
do: Swap long formal words for daily words
Cute or funny names for spirits and monsters
avoid: Long compound words
Folklore ghosts known for gore

title: Thai loanwords: keep the common ones, avoid long transliterated names
text: Some English words are normal Thai: บอส, ด่าน, เกม, ทีม. But transliterated names like "เดอะ ฟรอสต์ วอร์เดน" are hard to read and sound awkward; give a Thai name with meaning instead ("ผู้คุมน้ำแข็ง"). Prefer "จุด" over "เช็คพอยต์", "ภารกิจ" over "มิชชั่น", "คะแนน" over "พอยต์". Brand and product names stay in their official form.
use_when: a Thai game whose ideas came from English, or translating names
do: Make a Thai name with meaning for each boss or place
Keep official brand spellings as given
avoid: Spelling English names in Thai letters
English words mixed into every line

title: Thai particles: none in labels, light ones on the intro card
text: ครับ and ค่ะ give the game's voice a gender and add length, so leave them out of labels, chapter lines and rules. On the intro card and goal, a light นะ, เลย or กัน adds warmth: "ไปช่วยกันเลย!", "ระวังวงแดงนะ". Do not stack them ("นะคะจ๊ะ"). Use even fewer for teens and adults.
use_when: any Thai text, especially labels and rules
do: Zero particles in labels
At most one soft particle per sentence on the card
avoid: ครับ or ค่ะ at the end of rules
Baby-talk particles for teens

title: Thai lines with a balanced rhythm or internal rhyme stick
text: Thai ears love two balanced halves and a sound echo (สัมผัส): "ข้ามสะพาน ผ่านม่านหมอก", "จุดเทียน เวียนรอบเจดีย์", "หนีให้ไว ไฟไล่หลัง". Use it on the intro card, the goal or 1-2 key labels, not everywhere, and only while the line stays short. A rhyme that forces a strange word is worse than no rhyme.
use_when: Thai intro cards, goals and key labels for any audience
do: Two halves of 3-5 syllables
Use the rhyme on the climax label
avoid: Forced rhymes with odd words
A rhyme on every label (sounds like a chant)

title: Thai sacred places and objects get respectful verbs only
text: Temples, Buddha images, spirit houses, monks and the royal family must never be enemies, hazards, tactics targets or things to break, steal or kick. Use respectful verbs: "ไหว้ศาลพระภูมิ", "จุดธูปที่วัด", "ไปกราบพระ". Folk spirits can be playful opponents; sacred objects are places of safety or blessing in the story.
use_when: Thai temple, spirit or folklore themes
do: Make sacred places the safe goal or a blessing stop
Use ไหว้, กราบ, จุดธูป beside temple scenery
avoid: A Buddha image as a boss, hazard or tactics target
Monks as guards to sneak past

title: English for UK audiences: British spelling and words, plain sentences
text: When lang = en and the players are in the UK, use British spelling and words: colour, centre, metre, sweets (not candy), queue, torch (not flashlight), mum. Keep sentences short and literal; UK families respond well to gentle understatement and dry humour ("The dragon is mildly annoyed."). Avoid American sports metaphors and dollar signs.
use_when: lang = en and the venue or players are in the UK
do: British spelling on the card and labels
Light dry humour for families and adults
avoid: US terms (candy, flashlight, mom)
Hype words on every line ("AWESOME!")

title: Switching language: rewrite the line, do not translate word for word
text: A label that works in English may be long or flat in Thai, and Thai rhymes vanish in English. When the same game is made in both languages, keep the meaning, the count and the names, then write each line fresh: "Ring the old bell" becomes "ตีระฆังเก่า", "Cross the misty bridge" becomes "ข้ามสะพานหมอก". Puns and rhymes are rewritten as new ones or dropped.
use_when: a creator wants both th and en versions, or a comment asks to change lang
do: Keep the same number of labels and the same names
Re-check length limits in the new language
avoid: Literal translations that keep English word order in Thai
An English pun spelled in Thai letters

title: Voice for kids 6-10: warm, playful, clear, one idea per line
text: Kids follow concrete, kind tasks: helping animals, finding friends, waking sleepy giants. Use exclamations warmly but sparingly ("Help the baby turtles home!"), make villains silly rather than evil ("the Grumpy Snow Troll"), and keep every line one idea. Parents often read the card aloud, so it must sound good spoken.
use_when: players are kids 6-10
do: Helping and finding verbs
Silly villains, cute captives
avoid: Death, blood or real-world fears (getting lost, strangers)
Sarcasm and irony

title: Voice for teens: confident, a little dangerous, never talking down
text: Teens switch off at baby words and over-explaining. Write short, cool lines with real stakes: "Nobody leaves the fog. Except you." Labels can be terse ("Past the hounds", "Don't look back"). Mild menace and dry jokes work; cute mascots and "Great job!" do not. Make the challenge explicit: time, rank, the leaderboard.
use_when: players are teens 13-17, school groups or youth events
do: Terse labels and a bold boss name
Mention the leaderboard or time in a race
avoid: Childish words and exclamation marks everywhere
Lectures or morals on the card

title: Voice for families: sayable aloud, so parents can cheer and hint
text: In MR, parents watch from the side and call out. Labels with a clear, shoutable noun let them join in ("Go to the bell!", "The duck, the duck!"). Keep scares mild, make humour work on two levels (a pun for parents, a silly image for kids) and use "together" words when play is together. Avoid anything a parent would have to explain afterwards.
use_when: players are families, or parents watch from the side
do: A visible, nameable noun in every label
Humour that works for both ages
avoid: Hidden-meaning labels spectators cannot follow
Scary content that needs a parental warning

title: Voice for adults: atmosphere and wit, still short
text: Adults enjoy tone: dread, irony, nostalgia, a mystery. Lines can carry mood words ("The tide brings back what it took.") and boss names can be grim ("The Drowned Abbot"). They still read in a headset, so length limits do not change. Adults at events are often first-time VR players too, so keep the rules plain even when the story is rich.
use_when: players are adults: events, date nights, corporate groups
do: One mood word per line
Let the mystery or irony sit on the intro card
avoid: Long literary sentences
Assuming adults know game jargon

title: Voice for brands: the product is the hero object, not ad copy
text: A brand game reads like a story, not a banner. Make the product or mascot a visible hero object (the golden bottle at the summit, the mascot to free) and use the brand name at most in the title and on the intro card. Labels stay story beats ("Climb to the golden bottle"), never slogans. Follow the brand's words-to-avoid exactly and make no health or price claims.
use_when: a brand, sponsor or product launch brief
do: Brand name in the title or card only
The product as the final checkpoint or the portal's meaning
avoid: Slogans or prices in labels
Product claims the creator did not give

title: Voice for educators: one true idea per label, the story carries the lesson
text: In a school game each checkpoint can teach one simple fact through its label and scenery: "Visit Mars, the red planet", "Find the coral that feeds the fish". Keep facts short, true and checkable; if unsure, use a story label instead. The intro card frames learning as a mission ("Your rocket must visit 5 planets"), not a test.
use_when: educators, school trips or learning goals in the brief
do: One short, true fact per label
Frame learning as a mission
avoid: Quiz questions in labels (players cannot answer)
Facts you are not sure about

title: Voice for first-time VR players: reassure, then invite
text: Newcomers worry about the headset more than the game. The intro card can open calmly ("Look around. The floor has changed, the room has not.") and the rules should say plainly what touching and finishing look like. Keep the first label easy and close ("Step to the first light") so the first success comes within seconds.
use_when: players are new to VR or MR
do: A calm first sentence on the card
A first label that is obvious and near
avoid: Opening with danger or a countdown
Jargon like "spawn", "hitbox", "HUD"
source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

title: Fantasy: name the role and give it a title
text: Fantasy (being someone else) lives in the role words. Open the card with a titled role ("You are the Ember Knight", "เราคือผู้ถือตะเกียงคนสุดท้าย") and let labels be the role's duties ("Guard the shrine"). The boss should be the role's natural enemy. A role without a title is just "the player".
use_when: fantasy is a top feeling in the brief
do: A role with a title in sentence 1 or 2
Labels that are the role's duties
avoid: Calling the player "user" or "player" in the story
Roles that need abilities the genre lacks (a wizard who casts spells in a runner)

title: Submission (relaxing): soft verbs, no threats, no clocks
text: A relaxing game uses calm verbs (wander, visit, light, rest) and gentle images (lanterns on water, a sleepy cat, falling petals). Leave out timeLimit, alarm words and villains. Hazards, if any, become gentle things to step around (puddles, sleeping frogs). The intro card can invite rather than command: "Take a slow walk through the lantern garden."
use_when: submission is a top feeling, or players are seniors or anxious first-timers
do: Invitation wording on the card
Calm, sensory nouns in labels
avoid: Countdowns, "hurry", "danger"
A boss-style climax

title: Discovery: hint, do not spoil
text: Discovery labels promise without giving away: "Follow the glow", "Behind the waterfall", "Peek into the old well". The scenery beside that checkpoint delivers the surprise. The intro card should say there are secrets to see, not list them. Keep at least one surprise vignette that no label mentions.
use_when: discovery is a top feeling
do: Labels as invitations
One unlabelled surprise in the scenery
avoid: Labels that name the surprise ("See the giant octopus")
Hint labels in a race

title: Fellowship words must not promise teamwork the engine lacks
text: A shared floor lets players see each other's avatars and a race ranks them; there are no shared tasks, hand-offs or team scores. So write "together" as a shared journey ("Walk the ghost road together"), not as cooperation ("Lift the gate together", "One player holds the lamp"). Spectator cheering is real fellowship in MR: invite it on the card.
use_when: fellowship is a feeling, or play_mode is together
do: "Together" as a shared journey
Invite spectators to cheer
avoid: Tasks that need two players
Team scores or roles per player

title: Sensation: short punchy lines and sensory nouns
text: Sensation games sell the wow, so text should be brief and physical: "Lava below. Steady steps.", "Into the storm!", "สะพานลอยฟ้า ค่อยๆ เดิน". Pair the words with the strongest visual at that checkpoint (void floor, giant models, neon). One exclamation mark per line at most.
use_when: sensation is a top feeling, especially with void floor or big hero models
do: Sensory nouns: fire, ice, height, light
Put the punchiest label at the most dramatic spot
avoid: Long explanations
Wow words with no wow scenery beside them

title: Use second person "you are" and keep the player silent
text: Story text speaks to the player as "you" and gives them a role: "You are the night ranger." The player character never speaks, so never write lines for them ("I must hurry!") and never quote other characters as if they talk back. First- or third-person narration ("The hero walked...") distances players who are physically walking the route.
use_when: writing any intro card, chapter line or board story
do: "You are..." early on the card
Imperatives in labels ("Free the fox")
avoid: First-person lines for the player
Narration about "the hero" in third person

title: Pick a role that fits the genre's main verb
text: Runner roles walk and visit: lantern carrier, ghost hunter on patrol, courier, explorer, pilgrim, rescuer. Battle roles fight with a sword and dodge: knight, temple guardian, ice ranger, monster hunter. Tactics roles are the piece: a jumping rider (knight), a sliding monk (bishop), a charging cart (rook), the queen. A ghost hunter in a runner "checks the haunted spots"; in battle she "cuts down the ghosts".
use_when: choosing the player role for an option or the build
do: Match the role's main verb to the genre engine
Use the same role across labels, chapters and the card
avoid: A sniper or wizard role (no shooting or spells)
A runner role that fights

title: Show a character's wish through the label, not through speech
text: Characters cannot talk, but the label can carry what they want: "Bring Grandma her lost cat", "Wake the sleepy giant for the harvest", "พาลูกช้างไปหาแม่". Place the character model beside the checkpoint so players connect the want to a face. One clear want per character, and at most 2-3 named characters in a short game.
use_when: the brief has characters the player should care about
do: Want + who in one label
The character model next to their checkpoint
avoid: Quoted speech ("Grandma: Find my cat!") that reads as dialogue
More than 3 named characters

title: Vignettes tell what happened: show the aftermath beside the label
text: Scenery tells story without words when it shows a result: a tipped cart and spilled fruit beside "Follow the thief's trail", broken lanterns beside "Relight the path", a sleeping dragon beside "Tiptoe past the dragon". In the layout brief, name the vignette for each labelled checkpoint so the words and the picture say the same thing.
use_when: writing the layout brief for a story runner
do: One vignette per key label, described in the layout brief
Aftermath props (broken, spilled, frozen, sleeping)
avoid: Labels with no scenery support
Vignettes that contradict the label
source: Schell, The Art of Game Design

title: Make the goal visible from the spawn: a landmark that pulls players in
text: Place the story's goal as the tallest or brightest model, seen from the start: the tower with the last bell, the volcano, the moon gate. The intro card names it ("Reach the moon gate"), and players see the promise the whole walk. In MR keep it inside the play area and away from real walls so it stays in view.
use_when: a runner with a journey or climax, writing the layout brief
do: Name the landmark on the card and in the layout brief
Put it near the portal or the last checkpoint
avoid: A goal hidden until the last second in a narrative walk
A landmark outside the play area in MR

title: The lighting preset and the story must say the same time and mood
text: A Land has one lighting preset, so the story must fit it: night or spooky with midnight ghosts, morning with a journey starting, evening with lanterns and going home, neon with a future city, noon with bright festivals. Do not write "the sun sets as you walk"; the light will not change. In MR daylight, avoid stories that need darkness.
use_when: choosing lighting and writing the story card
do: Name the time of day the preset shows
Pick spooky or night only indoors or after dark in MR
avoid: Stories where the light changes during play
A midnight story on a sunny outdoor MR floor

title: Give red circles a red fiction: fire, lava, curse, alarm
text: Runner hazards always look like red circles and battle warnings are red rings, so name them as something red or warning: lava pools, fire pits, curse rings, alarm zones, angry ant nests, dragon fire. Water or ice names fight the colour. Use one hazard name across the card, the rules and the layout brief ("lava pools" everywhere).
use_when: naming hazards or warning rings in a story
do: A red fiction
The same name in rules and layout brief
avoid: Calling red circles "icy puddles"
A different hazard name on every line

title: In MR, write the real room into the story
text: Players see the real walls, windows and people, so the story should explain them: the walls are "the castle walls", the crowd is "the villagers watching", the window light is "the moon outside". One sentence on the intro card is enough: "The villagers watch from the hall. Show them the ghosts are gone." This turns the real room from a distraction into part of the world.
use_when: an MR game in a visible real space with spectators
do: One intro sentence that names the real surroundings in story terms
Treat spectators as an audience in the fiction
avoid: A setting the room clearly contradicts ("deep under the sea") with no framing
Giving spectators a story task

title: Void floor needs a story reason: a bridge, a sky island, a cliff path
text: The void floor turns the real floor into a bottomless drop, which is dramatic and dizzy. Justify it in words so it feels intended: "The bridge over the abyss", "Islands in the clouds", "สะพานข้ามเหว". Keep labels calm and reassuring on void sections ("Steady steps"), and never write lines that dare players to jump or look down while walking fast.
use_when: a design using void floor
do: Name the height in the story
Calm wording on void stretches
avoid: "Jump!" or "Look down!" labels
Void floor for kids or first-time VR without a gentle story
source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

title: Story props that a label names cannot be VR-only
text: Decor marked "VR only" is hidden in MR. If a label points at a prop ("Wake the dragon"), that prop must be visible in MR, or the label points at empty floor. Use VR-only decor for background mood (sky, far walls, extra trees) and keep every story prop named by a label as normal scenery.
use_when: an MR layout brief with story props and VR-only decor
do: Keep labelled story props visible in MR
Use VR-only for distant backdrop
avoid: A labelled hero prop set to VR only
Relying on hidden props to tell the story

title: Humour: about one joke in every 3-4 lines, carried by the nouns
text: Humour lands best in silly nouns and situations, not in wordplay that must be read twice: "Wake the snoring goat", "the Grumpy Cabbage King", "ปลุกแพะนอนกรน". Use about one funny line per 3-4 lines so the story still moves; a joke on every label tires players. Put the biggest laugh on the boss name or the last label.
use_when: a light, family or kids game, or a comedy brief
do: Silly creatures and objects in labels
One running joke across the game
avoid: Puns that only work in one language
Humour that mocks people, accents or cultures

title: Wonder: build up with small sights, end on one big one
text: Wonder needs contrast. Let early labels be small and close ("Follow the fireflies"), then reveal a big sight with a big word near the end ("Under the sky whale"). Pair the wonder label with the largest model or the void floor. If every label says "amazing", nothing is.
use_when: sensation or discovery games, all ages
do: Small to big across the route
Save one wonder word for the climax
avoid: "Amazing" or "magical" on every line
The biggest sight right at the spawn

title: Mild scare: dread in words and light, never sudden shocks
text: In MR, sudden scares make people run into real walls, so scare with mood, not jumps. Words do the work: "Something follows the lanterns", "Do not wake her". Use spooky or night lighting indoors, slow-reveal ghost models beside labels and a warm, safe ending ("Back to the light"). For kids, let the scary thing turn out friendly or silly by the last label.
use_when: spooky, ghost or horror themes, especially in MR or for kids
do: Dread words + spooky lighting + a warm ending
For kids, reveal the ghost is friendly at the end
avoid: "Run!" labels or chase framing in MR
Gore, death or jump-scare promises
source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

title: Heroism: raise the stakes one step each chapter or board
text: Heroism grows when each step matters more: chapter 1 saves a farm, chapter 3 the town, the boss the kingdom. State the stake in a few words in each line ("The village is next.") and give the player the credit in the final line ("Only you stand at the gate."). Do not open at maximum stakes; there is nowhere left to go.
use_when: battle or tactics with fantasy or challenge, or a heroic runner
do: Rising stakes across chapters or boards
The player as the one who decides it at the end
avoid: Saving the world in chapter 1
Ending with someone else saving the day

title: Worked runner card (English, families): The Lantern River
text: Story: "The river spirits lost their lights. You are the lantern child. Light 5 lanterns before the mist covers the river, then cross home." Goal: "Light 5 lanterns, then step through the moon gate." Rules: "Walk to the lanterns in order", "Walk, do not run", "Red circles are fire pits: they send you back", "Finish at the moon gate". Labels: "Lantern 1: the jetty", "Lantern 2: the reeds", "Past the sleeping frog", "Lantern 3: the old boat", "Lantern 4: the willow", "Last lantern: the bridge".
use_when: a reference shape for a family runner card (do not copy)
do: Match counts across story, goal and labels
Mix numbered set labels with one moment label
avoid: Copying this text for a different brief

title: Worked runner card (Thai, school kids): rescue the baby elephants
text: Story: "ลูกช้าง 4 ตัวหลงป่าตอนพายุมา เราคือผู้พิทักษ์ป่าตัวน้อย ไปพาลูกช้างกลับหาแม่กันเลย!" Goal: "ช่วยลูกช้างครบ 4 ตัว แล้วเดินเข้าประตูป่า" Rules: "เดินไปตามจุดที่เรืองแสงทีละจุด", "เดินนะ ห้ามวิ่ง", "อย่าเหยียบวงแดง (รังมดแดง)". Labels: "ข้ามลำธาร", "ช่วยลูกช้างตัวแรก", "ลอดใต้ต้นไทร", "ช่วยตัวที่ 2", "ช่วยตัวที่ 3", "ช่วยตัวสุดท้าย".
use_when: a reference shape for a Thai kids runner card (do not copy)
do: Spoken Thai with เรา and one particle
Digits for counts
avoid: Copying this text for a different brief

title: Worked battle text (lava theme, teens): from chapters to boss
text: Story: "The Ash King woke under the mountain and his hounds took the road. You are the last ember knight. Fight up the mountain and end him." Chapters: "The Ash Road" / "Imps pour out of the cracks." (grunts); "The Shield Gate" / "Stone guards lock shields. Hit them from the side." (shields + grunts); "Ember Storm" / "Fire falls from the sky. Keep moving." (rain); "The Hound Pit" / "His hounds smell you." (beast + grunts). Boss: "The Ash King" / "The Ash King rises from his throne. Break his crown."
use_when: a reference shape for battle chapters and the boss (do not copy)
do: One foe meaning per chapter line
The boss named on the card first
avoid: Copying this text for a different brief

title: Worked tactics text (heist, adults): The Moonstone Job
text: Story: "Five moonstones sit in the duke's palace and his night watch never sleeps. You are the thief who becomes whatever the job needs. Take the stones in order and do not get caught." Boards: knight "Leap the garden hedges and take 2 stones."; rook "Charge down the long hall before the watch turns."; bishop "Slip along the chapel diagonals."; queen with king "The duke himself. Corner him for the last stone."
use_when: a reference shape for tactics board stories (do not copy)
do: A piece role tied to each place
The king on the last board
avoid: Copying this text for a different brief

title: Worked MR battle text (Thai, families, forest): the firefly forest
text: Story: "ป่าหิ่งห้อยโดนเงามืดบุก เราคือองครักษ์ป่า ดาบอยู่ในมือขวาแล้ว ปกป้องหิ่งห้อยไว้ให้ได้!" Chapters (at most 6 foes each in MR): "ชายป่า" / "เงาตัวเล็กวิ่งเข้ามา"; "กำแพงโล่" / "ทหารเงาถือโล่ ฟันด้านข้างนะ"; "ฝนหนาม" / "หนามตกจากฟ้า ก้าวหลบให้ทัน". Boss: "ราชาเงามืด" / "ราชาเงามืดมาแล้ว ไล่มันออกไปจากป่า!" Rules include "ก้าวออกจากวงแดง ไม่ต้องวิ่ง".
use_when: a reference shape for MR battle text in Thai (do not copy)
do: Step-not-run wording in MR
Short Thai lines under about 30 characters
avoid: Copying this text for a different brief

title: Labels that promise mechanics: open, carry, shoot, choose
text: Writers slip in verbs from other games: "Open the chest", "Carry the egg to the nest", "Shoot the target", "Choose your path". The engine only knows touching checkpoints in order, so players try the action and nothing happens. Rewrite as arrivals: "Reach the chest", "Visit the nest", "Pass the targets", and give a single route with no choices.
use_when: reviewing labels, chapter lines or board stories
do: Rewrite every hand or choice verb as an arrival verb
Keep branching out of all text
avoid: "Choose" or "or" in labels
Verbs that need buttons in an MR runner

title: Generic names ("Dark Lord", "Magic Forest") make the game forgettable
text: Names are the cheapest way to make a world feel specific. Replace "Dark Lord" with "the Rust Abbot", "Magic Forest" with "Whisper Woods", "ป่ามหัศจรรย์" with "ป่าหิ่งห้อย". Make each name concrete (a material, an animal, a sound, a local place) and tie it to the theme and palette.
use_when: naming places, bosses, the title or the role
do: Concrete noun + theme word
Local flavour for Thai themes (ตลาดน้ำ, ดอย, ลำธาร)
avoid: Fantasy clichés with no detail
Names copied from famous games or films
